title: "Have" isn't a verb
goal: Expressing possession and company with the *-тай / -тэй / -той* suffix — how Mongolian says "have" with no verb at all.
bekal: say what you have and don't have
tell apart three ways of expressing possession and pick the natural one

dialogs.title: Яриа — Нохойтой хүн
dialogs.intro: Budi visits Sarnai's home. There's a big dog in the yard, and the conversation moves from there to everything in the house.

notes: ⚠️ **Mongolian has no verb "to have".** Instead, the *-тай* suffix attaches to **the thing**, not to the owner. *Би нохой**той*** is literally "I (am) with-dog" — and the owner isn't marked at all. This is a genuinely new idea for English speakers, and it takes about a week to feel natural.
**Its opposite is -гүй, which you know from unit 11.** *Нохойтой* (has a dog) versus *нохойгүй* (has no dog). These two suffixes work as a pair and handle all of possession.

**The same suffix also means "with (someone)" and "and".** *Бидэн**тэй*** (with us), *ах**тайгаа*** (with his big brother), *цай**тай** талх* (bread with tea). One suffix, two meanings that are really one: "accompanied by".

⚠️ **Цайтай юу, цайгүй юу? is a question you'll hear in almost every Mongolian home.** Literally "with tea or without tea?", it means "would you like tea?" Answering *цайтай* means yes. ⚠️ Refusing outright is considered impolite; if you're not thirsty, accept and take a sip.
**Ганцаараа = alone**, from *ганц* (only one) + the suffix *-аараа*. The same pattern forms *хоёулаа* (the two of us), *гурвуулаа* (the three of us) — the *-уулаа / -үүлээ* suffix you saw in unit 3.

grammars.title: Three ways to express possession
body: Mongolian has three ways, and each is used for something different. This table shows how they divide up — read the last column first.

head: Way
Example
Meaning
Used for
rows: Something present right now, which can change.
Describes the thing; doesn't state ownership.
I haven't got any money (on me).

after: ⚠️ **The difference matters and is easy to feel.** *Би мөнгөтэй* means "I'm well-off" — a quality. *Надад мөнгө байна* means "I've got money on me" — a state. If a friend asks whether you can pay for lunch, the answer is the second.
**At A1, use -тай for almost everything.** The *-д байна* form will come naturally through use, and mixing the two up never stops people from understanding you.

grammars.title: The -тай suffix as an adjective maker
body: This is the use that makes this suffix one of the most productive tools in Mongolian: it turns **any noun** into an adjective, with no new words to memorize.
after: **Look at the eighth row.** The goodbye word *баяртай* you learned in unit 1 is really just "joyful" — a wish, not a greeting. Mongolian says goodbye by wishing people stay happy, just as English "goodbye" was once "God be with you".

⚠️ **You can make your own adjectives with this pattern, and people will understand you.** If you know *хүч* (strength), you can say *хүчтэй* (strong) without ever having learned it. This saves hundreds of words of memorizing — use it boldly.

blocks.title: Asking "do you have …?"
items: *Чи машинтай юу?* — Do you have a car?
*Танайх нохойтой юу?* — Does your family have a dog?
⚠️ A one-word short answer is enough: *Тийм* or *Үгүй* — or, more naturally, by repeating: *Машинтай.* / *Машингүй.*

blocks.text: ⚠️ The last two rows add **-гаа / -гээ**, the "one's own" suffix covered fully in unit 17. The difference matters: *найзтай* means "with a friend (anyone)", while *найзтайгаа* means "with **my own** friend". Mongolians almost always use the second form when talking about people close to them, and leaving it out sounds cold.

head: Sentence
Meaning
rows: I watched a movie with my friend.
I talked with my mother on the phone.

sections.title: The home and what's in it

blocks.text: ⚠️ **Зуух is a matter of life and death in Mongolia.** The iron stove in the middle of a ger burns coal or wood, and it has to be refilled several times a night when the temperature drops to −30°C. Family members take turns getting up to feed it. If you stay in a ger, your host will do it for you, and you needn't feel guilty — it's the host's job.

blocks.title: The bankhar dog
items: *Банхар* is the Mongolian herding dog breed — big, thick-coated, and a herder's companion for thousands of years.

⚠️ **Never walk up to a ger without calling out from a distance.** The standard phrase you must say: ***Нохой хорь!*** (no-KHOI khor') — "Hold the dog!" It isn't a sign of fear but the right, polite way to announce your arrival.
The phrase works exactly like knocking on a door. The host will come out, hold the dog, and invite you in.
Mongolians don't knock on a ger door. You call out, then go in — without waiting for an answer, because an unlocked door means guests are always welcome.
I watched a movie with my friend.
